title: Evidence in Two Days (sample)
description: A short sample audio course: relevance on Day 1, hearsay on Day 2. It uses every listen/v1 segment type.

segments.say: Welcome to Day 1. Today is about relevance, the first gate every piece of evidence has to pass.
Under FRE 401, evidence is relevant if (a) it has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable, and (b) that fact is of consequence. Both are required.
Courts call it a low bar, e.g. Knapp v. State, 168 Ind. 153 (1907), where the defendant's story was relevant to his fear even though no one proved it true.
So a photo of the intersection is relevant even if it only helps a little?
Exactly. Any tendency is enough. The fight comes later, under Rule 403.

segments.ask: Evidence moves a fact of consequence only slightly. Is it relevant under Rule 401?
segments.answer: Yes. Any tendency suffices; weight is for the jury.

segments.say: Rule 403 lets the court exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice, confusion, or waste of time. The factors are weighed together.

segments.ask: Which way does Rule 403 lean: toward admitting or excluding?
segments.answer: Toward admitting. The danger must substantially outweigh the probative value.

segments.say: Hearsay under FRE 801(c) is (1) a statement, (2) made out of court, (3) offered to prove the truth of what it asserts. All three are required.
Rule 803(2), the excited utterance, lets in a statement about a startling event made while under the stress of it.

segments.ask: Is a statement offered only to show the listener had notice hearsay?
segments.answer: No. It is not offered for its truth.
